newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident politician may be free next week.
newsitem.headline: China dissident politician may be free next week.

text.p: China may free the most senior official jailed for the 1989 student-led pro-democracy protests from months of house arrest after his family agreed to move from their government residence, relatives said on Thursday.
"We are very happy," said one member of the family of Bao Tong. "We may be reunited with him next week. That is what the authorities have said."

Authorities had insisted Bao's family move from their government-allocated apartment in a block reserved for high-ranking officials before they would free the former aide to Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang from house arrest.
"We plan to move house next week and that was the condition the authorities had set before they would allow Bao Tong to come home," said the family member who declined to be identified.
"He is very happy because he will soon be reunited with his family after all this time," the family member said.
Bao was released from jail in May 1996 after serving seven years in prison for his role in the 1989 demonstrations, and immediately placed under house arrest in the suburbs of Beijing.
Bao's wife and daughter would move to an ordinary apartment in Shijingshan in the western suburbs of Beijing next week, the relative said.
Bao held ministerial status when he was secretary to the Communist Party's powerful Politburo in the late 1980s.
He was the most senior official to be jailed for his role in the 1989 Tiananmen Square demonstrations that were crushed by the army on June 4 that year with heavy loss of life.
Bao was convicted of leaking state secrets by passing information that notified the students that the government planned to impose martial law in Beijing in late May.

"The most important thing now is to make sure that he receives proper and adequate medical treatment," the relative said. "It was very inconvenient for him to see a doctor when he was in the Western Hills but now this should be easier."
He had been treated for a variety of ailments while in prison but this had lapsed after he was released last May and moved to a state dormitory in the Western Hills near Beijing.
Bao has been held virtually incommunicado except for occasional visits from his wife.

"We don't yet know if there will be any conditions attached to his going home," the relative said. "The officials have not yet specified any conditions except moving house but that does not mean that they won't set some in the future."

Diplomats say Bao is a source of anxiety for China's leaders, who fear he may reveal details of the dealings of the highest party and government echelons in the weeks before the bloody crackdown on demonstrators.
Bao's case has drawn fire from the United States, which has protested against his continued detention without recourse to judicial representation and without access to his family.
Chinese officials have defended Bao's detention, saying the measures were necessary and required by law.
A two-year suspension of his political rights applies to Bao after the end of his jail term, meaning he would not be allowed to speak to reporters or to publish.
